speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Vezina (Minister of State (Employment and Immigration)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Employment and Immigration)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, tomorrow we shall take one more step towards genuine employment equity in Canada.
As you know, the Employment Equity Act was passed in 1986. Under this legislation, all federally-regulated businesses which have 100 or more employees are required to submit an annual report on employment equity. The first series of annual reports is to be submitted not later than tomorrow, June 1.
For the very first time we will have information on the occupational levels and remuneration of four groups designated under the Employment Equity Act: women, Native people, members of visible minorities and disabled persons.
Judging from the reaction of employers, it is clear they are spending quite a bit of time and money to comply with the provisions of the legislation. They are aware of the benefits of, and the need for, improved employment equity in this country.
Before I continue my speech, Mr. Speaker, I would like to pay tribute to my colleague, the Minister of Communications
(Miss MacDonald), who played a key role in introducing and preparing the Employment Equity Act. Thanks to her efforts as Minister of Employment and Immigration, we can now enjoy the benefits of this legislation.
Under the legislation, all federally-regulated employers, Crown corporations as well as private sector businesses, are required to eliminate employment barriers, to adopt special measures and to make arrangements to accomodate certain differences. As a result, the designated groups will be able to meet the competitive challenge in the workplace. Until now, these groups have not been given a fair chance. Special measures are therefore necessary to help them close the gap.
Under the legislation, the employers concerned, mostly in the fields of banking, transportation and communications, must identify and remove barriers to the employment and promotion of women, Native people, members of visible minorities and disabled persons.
Employers must make an effort to achieve equitable representation in their work force. To that end, they must ensure that designated groups are represented in all occupations and at all levels of their organization. Their annual reports must indicate the rate of representation of designated groups according to occupational categories and salary ranges; they must also report on hirings, promotions and terminations of target group members.
Subsequently, we will verify, process and analyse these reports. They will be published and made available to the persons concerned across Canada. Later this year, I shall table in the House my first annual report on employment equity.
Mr. Speaker, our country was built on diversity. Nevertheless, the Abella Royal Commission showed us that there exists in Canadian workplaces a system that has always denied the very existence of such diversity.
As Rosalie Abella said in her report, "It is not that individuals in the designated groups are inherently unable to achieve equality on their own, it is that the obstacles in their way are so formidable and self-perpetuating that they cannot be overcome without intervention."
Systematic discrimination excludes members of certain groups through rules or employment customs that have nothing to do with the position or that are unnecessary for sound, effective management.
It is a fact that the unemployment rate for the groups covered by the Act tends to be higher than for other Canadians

May 31, 1988
Statements by Ministers
and many members of the target groups are underemployed. This situation well explains and justifies our action.
Employment equity programs do not restrain a company's growth, far from it. Making the most of the available skills and talents is a key to success.
The Employment Equity Act affects some 450 employers and more than 800,000 employees. The employers affected are required to develop and implement a complete employment equity program. In every region of the country, Employment and Immigration Canada has competent consultants who have helped them develop their programs and write the required reports.
We know that it has not been an easy task. Many employers experienced difficulties. But the worst is behind us. This first year will serve as a reference point. We are only beginning. I am sure that next June, employers will be better prepared. In the meantime, employment equity consultants from Employment and Immigration Canada can help them.
In 1986, to complement the Act, the Government created another employment equity program, for federal contracts, to encourage firms doing business with the federal Government to make their staff representative. Companies with at least 100 employees that wish to bid on government contracts for goods and services worth $200,000 or more must commit themselves to implementing employment equity. Furthermore, this commitment is part of the offer. So far, more than 1,000 firms have made this commitment.
The lack of contract compliance can result in the offer being rejected. In early 1987, as Minister of Supply and Services, I had to use this coercive power. Several companies had been asked to bid on a contract. They all sent their submission without the commitment to employment equity. Therefore, we refused to award this contract.
Employers who are awarded a contract can be audited on their premises by officials from Employment and Immigration Canada. Contractors who do not respect the signed commitment can be denied the opportunity to bid on other contracts. Employment and Immigration Canada consultants are also at their disposal to provide them with the necessary advice and assistance.
Government procurement is thus an important lever in implementing our employment equity policy. Through it, we can extend the principle of fairness defended by this program to areas of activity that it would have been quite impossible for us to reach.
Mr. Speaker, equity in the workplace will not be achieved overnight. It is a slow, sometimes painful process that takes patience and constant cooperation from all concerned. Nevertheless, I am convinced that thanks to the innovative employment equity programs launched by our Government, we will get there.
[DOT] (mo)

Mr. Speaker, I cannot believe that for the second time in two days the Government has come out with a wonderful flowery statement which has absolutely no validity in fact. I refer to the opening of Access Awareness Week yesterday. That from a Government which is building superboxes which are inaccessible to the handicapped. Access Awareness Week was launched by a speech from a municipal politician who told the disabled not to try to integrate their transit system because it would be too expensive and would never happen.
Now we have this wonderful statement on employment equity. Let us look at the reality of the so-called employment equity legislation which was passed by the Government. The legislation has all the power of a water gun. In fact, a water gun is perhaps more powerful than the legislation. It has all the power of an inflated balloon because there is absolutely no enforcement mechanism.
Let us look at what is happening with companies which claim they are responding to Bill C-62. The Maritime Employers' Association, in the name of employment equity, claims that it is following the provisions of Bill C-62. Some longshoremen who have been working in the business for 10, 15, or 20 years are losing their status. Some of them are being forced to take tests, supposedly in the name of employment equity. I do not see that many women working as longshoremen. The employers are actually using this Bill to compromise the employment status of current employees while not responding to the need to integrate women and minorities into the work force.

Mr. Speaker, the truth is that it is a hard and rocky road. It is also true there have been a number of detours since this Government came to power, and I am referring specifically to the fact that in 1986, for the first time in Canada's history, the wage gap between men and women grew wider. Instead of narrowing because of the Government's efforts, it grew wider!

In 1986, for the first time since statistics were kept on this issue, the wage gap between men and women in this country became larger on a percentage basis.
The employment equity legislation could have had teeth and force if the Government had accepted the more than three dozen amendments proposed by the Liberal Party to try to give it some enforcement power. In fact, the Government brought in a shallow mechanism which has no substance. Even the Canadian Human Rights Commission, which is not a partisan opposition body, believes that the only way employment equity can really be enforced is if the Canadian Human Rights Act is given the teeth to force employers to pay women the same as men for work of equal value, something which does not exist at the moment.
May 31, 1988

While we appreciate the fine words and rhetoric in the same way as we appreciated the lovely concert on Sunday night which was going to make all things accessible to all Canadians, the federal Government has not directed a single penny toward municipalities which want to improve their infrastructure in order to make their streets and municipal buildings accessible. Not one penny of federal money has been directed toward access awareness on the ground where it really counts.
In the same way, this legislation has absolutely no possibility for enforcement because there is no penalty provided and no mechanism in place to ensure that employers go ahead with employment equity. That is why you see employers-

. .. like the Maritime Employers Association which claims to comply with Bill C-62 but tells its employees who have been employed for 10, 12 or 15 years that they have to take tests, and at the same time they don't hire minorities, women or visible minorities.
So why is this situation being tolerated? Mr. Speaker, it is being tolerated because the Government introduced a Bill, said it would do something to provide for employment equity, but failed to provide an enforcement mechanism.

This is like setting up a Criminal Code amendment and telling a bank robber that he is not allowed to rob a bank but if he does there is no penalty, take the money and run. How can you have an employment equity bill which has no enforcement mechanism, no penalty against employers who do not comply, and absolutely no structure in place to make sure that employers are complying? The only compliance requirement is that they report. They can report that they are doing nothing and that is fine, that is totally within the ambit of this phoney piece of legislation.
I am not particularly happy about this statement, Mr. Speaker. I am not happy about a series of statements which have come from the Government which are nothing more than flowery rhetoric. We should hang our heads in shame to think that in 1986, for the first time since statistics were kept, under this Government the wage gap between men and women got wider rather than narrower. If we do not do something by way of amendment to improve legislation, in 10 or 20 years from now we will be giving the same speeches in the House of Commons.

Yes, the road is hard and rocky, and it is a long road. We are nearing the twenty-first century, and nothing has been done because although the Government was willing to make some nice, impressive speeches, it did not want to act and use legislation to require employers to set up employment equity programs.
Statements by Ministers

That being said, Mr. Speaker, I certainly cannot endorse this statement.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister has made a statement on advances in employment equity as she sees them. She has spoken about the good things that will happen under the employment equity Bill. This is another case of rhetoric being put forward as the next election draws near to try to suggest to Canadians that a great deal has been accomplished when the reality is so very far from that. When those Canadians who are in the target groups; aboriginal peoples, the disabled, visible minorities, and women-to put them in alphabetical order rather than in order of the numbers of their groups-consider their situation and learn what the reports will tell them, they will know that the Government failed profoundly in Bill C-62 a couple of years ago in refusing to recognize the necessity of doing far more than calling for reports.
[DOT] (U20)
According to a Canadian Press report today, 70 per cent of the disabled are unemployed. The federal Government will discover those realities with respect to Crown corporations and areas under federal regulation upon which this legislation focuses, but what good will only having information about the shortcomings of employment do for those people?
The sad realities of inequity in employment in the past required far more action than is taking place. Of course, the Government tries to make much more of it.

The Minister said, and I quote:
Under this legislation all federally-regulated employees, Crown corporations
as well as private sector businesses, are required to eliminate employment
barriers, to adopt special measures and to make arrangements to accommodate
certain differences.
Actually, the legislation only requires employers to submit these reports. It does not require them to prepare a longer term strategy.

The most profound failure in this employment equity Bill is the Government's failure to require an action plan by employers. It is not for lack of attempts by the New Democratic Party and the Liberal Opposition to amend the Bill and strengthen it in ways that we see this end result.
The Minister praised her colleague, the former Minister of Employment and Immigration, the Minister of Communications (Miss MacDonald), who introduced the Bill. She stubbornly stood by the draft that had been put forward. While there were some minor amendments, the major amendments required to make this a genuine employment equity Bill were refused. The Minister's colleagues stood by that Bill and refused to make the required changes. Therefore, there is no point in joining the Minister in any praise for her

May 31, 1988
Committee Reports
colleague or in any great recognition of what the Government has done.
There is a great desire to make much of the reporting aspect and it would be very hard to top the Minister's statement this morning as a celebration of what reporting might achieve. We will learn what are the actual shortcomings and inequities and that this information will be rapidly digested and made available.
The Minister will make a statement and the reports will be made available throughout the country for people to buy. I only ask in passing how much these reports will cost lobby groups and those who wish to maintain the pressure. I hope the price will be quite low and that the information will be made available as quickly as possible so there will be no long delays that will enable employers to say that reports on their lack of progress toward equality are out of date. If there is too long a delay it will be too easy for employers to say that their circumstances have changed dramatically. There must be speedy action and abundant publicity about these reports to realize the potential the Minister has expressed about them.
There must be stronger provisions in the way of requirements on employers to take action. The Minister asserts that employers will take this action, but I am tempted to say this statement is in the long-standing Liberal tradition that by revealing the shortcomings of people they are motivated to correct them. Liberals have believed in that practice for too long, and it is distressing to see Conservatives practising the same short-sighted, indeed blind policy. People very often do not want to make a change unless they are compelled to do so.
Action plans must be required of employers so that they can stipulate the goals and targets they wish to achieve. Employers should be required to present their action plans to the agency that would actively monitor them to ensure that employment equity is actually achieved, as the Act claims it will do. Only if those steps are taken will those in the target groups and Canadians generally be sure that we will have more fairness in employment.
Another important aspect to consider is that the Bill is limited in its focus on Crown corporations and private enterprise under federal regulation. The Government has managed to keep itself clear of obligations to report and that refusal to take this responsibility is particularly regrettable. I believe employers who are facing these demands ought to be able to look to the federal Government to provide an example by revealing the shortcomings in employment in the federal Government and its institutions and then indicating targets and deadlines by which the situation concerning employment equity will be corrected.
I have seen figures for various groups setting limited goals and the shortcomings in information are quite obvious for a number of them. The statistics for the current situation in federal institutions are simply not available. The Treasury Board carried out a voluntary census among the various federal institutions. We cannot be sure how close those
statistics came to revealing the true situation, but the need to be quite clear about the situation for various groups leads me to call on the Government this morning to practice the same principles internally.
Surely the Treasury Board can act on these matters and take to itself the obligation to work under the employment equity Bill and ensure that leadership is being given to employers in the federal institutions.
I suggested during third reading debate a couple of years ago that it would be five years after a report before a government would be ready to take action. The next election may change this because we New Democrats would love to have the opportunity to make real progress toward employment equity. However, there is the possibility that years may pass before there is stronger legislation to make the kind of real progress to achieve employment equity that the Minister is claiming this morning will be the result of the present rather weak Bill.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
There are 19 motions in amendment on the Order Paper to amend Bill C-51, an Act to prohibit the advertising and promotion and respecting the labelling and monitoring of tobacco products. After deliberation, I am now ready to make a ruling with respect to their acceptability. All of these motions I find are in order.
Motions Nos. 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 all deal with advertising and will be grouped for debate and voted on as follows. If Motion No. 1 is carried, the question will not be put on Motion No. 2. A negative vote on Motion No. 1 necessitates a vote on Motion No. 2. An affirmative vote on Motion No. 2 will obviate the necessity of a vote on Motions Nos. 3 and 4. Motions Nos. 5 and 6 will be voted on separately.
Motions Nos. 7, 8, 9, 11 and 12 all deal with promotion and sponsorship. They will be grouped for debate and voted on as follows. An affirmative vote on Motion No. 7 will obviate the necessity of a vote on Motions Nos. 8 and 9. A negative vote on Motion No. 7 necessitates a vote on Motion No. 8. An affirmative vote on Motion No. 8 will obviate the necessity of a vote on Motion No. 9. A negative vote on Motion No. 8 necessitates a vote on Motion No. 9. Motions Nos. 11 and 12 will be voted on separately.
Motion No. 10 standing in the name of the Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell) is virtually the same as an amendment which was moved, debated and negatived in committee. Therefore in accordance with Standing Order 114(10), it will not be selected for debate in the House.
Motions Nos. 13, 14, 15 and 16 deal with reports, regulations, offences and punishments. They will be grouped for debate but voted on separately.
Motions Nos. 17, 18 and 19 dealing with the coming into force of the Bill, will be grouped for debate but voted on as follows. An affirmative vote on Motion No. 17 will obviate the necessity of a vote on Motion No. 18. A negative vote on Motion No. 17 necessitates a vote on Motion No. 18. Motion No. 19 will be voted on separately.
Agreed.

She said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in the debate on Bill C-51 with respect to the amendments. We have a number of amendments before us this morning. Some of them are housekeeping amendments, and some of them are more substantive. Let me get right to them.
The first motion is a very long and involved motion. Some aspects of it are merely housekeeping. I will not comment on those aspects of it. However, there is one part of Motion No. 1 which is not merely housekeeping. I am very concerned about it.
It is one that would change the wording: "No person shall advertise any tobacco product in Canada." to: "No person shall advertise any tobacco product offered for sale in Canada." This change in wording seems to indicate that one can advertise tobacco that is not for sale in Canada but which is for sale somewhere else. One might wonder why anyone would bother to do that if they cannot sell it in Canada. However, the result is that it is a promotion of tobacco and a promotion of smoking. It can have a generic effect of saying: "Tobacco is all right. It is even good for your health-nothing wrong with it".
This wording was much discussed in committee. The original wording was more along those lines, and we got rid of it. We changed the wording to close what would seem to be an inadvertent loophole which would permit advertising in Canada of products that are not for sale in Canada but nonetheless which would give the impression that tobacco products were just fine to buy. What we really need to get rid of is tobacco advertising, period.
We have to realize that in other countries loopholes have been used by tobacco companies. They have advertised lighters. They use the same logos and the same colours. By advertising lighters or matches, they are in effect advertising tobacco. Therefore, any loophole which is allowed in here can be a very serious one. I think we have to treat this as something that could weaken the impact of this much needed legislation.
My Motion No. 2 would restore to Bill C-51 the spirit that was approved at second reading. It changes the three year
May 31, 1988

phase-in of billboards to a date six months later than the second reading of Bill C-51. Bill C-51 was better in its original version in this respect. It was watered down to allow for this three year phase-in. I am suggesting that we go back to the original spirit of the law and bring it in much more quickly. When we consider that 35,000 Canadians are dying every year from tobacco related diseases and that the death toll from involuntary smoking is certainly in the hundreds, we should not be gingerly phasing in this ban on tobacco advertising but we should be working promptly to see that this encouragement of taking up a habit that kills people is ended as soon as possible.
With respect to Motion No. 3, if we must have a phase-in of billboard advertisements, this would reduce the amount of money that could be spent on advertising from two-thirds to one-half in the second year. That is relevant to current levels. This is a practical amendment. I would rather get rid of it completely and do so promptly. However, if we are going to have a phase-in let us at least reduce the amount, put limits on it so that it is clearly a phasing out and not an opportunity for advertising to continue at current levels.
Motion No. 4 is similar to Motion No. 3. It allows in the third year of the phase-in period a quarter of current billboard spending. Again, it is in the spirit of let us get rid of it and let us have clear caps on the amount of spending that would be permitted.
Motion No. 5 comes from the Government. It is a good amendment. It would tighten the loophole that is given to merchants to advertise tobacco names in their shop names, for example, "Lynn's Tobacco Shop". This type of advertising would not be permitted in radio and television ads, although it would be permitted in signs. The second part of the motion is merely housekeeping, and we would support that.
Finally, in the first set of amendments is Motion No. 6. This is one of my amendments and it would restore to the Bill the original date in the second reading version for the removal of in-store advertisements. Here again the original Bill was better. As a result of a lot of pressure put on by this very profitable industry that is killing people in the process of making money, unfortunately one result was that amendments were brought in at committee stage which weakened the provisions of this Bill.
The health community is looking at this Bill. It does not wish to see further amendments. That was said very clearly at committee stage. The health community considers this a minimal measure. At the municipal level there is legislation for the workplace, and here the Government has brought in no workplace legislation whatsoever. This is a very minimal action for advertising and for sponsorship. It is not complete. It is not thorough. It will go a long way, but we do not want it to be watered down any further.

The whole purpose of the amendments that I have brought in is to deal with some of these matters where there was too much watering down at committee, and get the Bill back on track to where it should be. The health community is saying: "Don't water it down any more. Let us take Bill C-51 as it is and let us get it into operation". Let us restore the spirit of the amendments that we agreed on earlier at second reading and get on with adopting this important piece of legislation.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. We played political leap-frog yesterday because the Government in its wisdom saw fit to ignore a chance to finally put Bill C-204 into law. In that regard, I wish to congratulate the efforts of the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald), who has shown an incredible intestinal fortitude in pursuing her Bill in the face of constant thwarting, confusion, and disinformation on the part of the Government. The reason I am shocked that we played this political leap-frog yesterday was that I expected, of course, that the Government was going to move with the Minister today to expedite Bill C-51. Although I cannot comment on the presence or absence of Members, I am shocked. Parliamentary secretaries can be hard working and well-intentioned, but I would have liked to hear from the Minister.
If one reads Motion No. 1, Subclause (3) I believe that this amendment has been moved specifically because of the free trade agreement. That amendment reads:
(3) For greater certainty, subsection (2) does not apply in respect of the distribution for sale of publications imported into Canada or the retransmission of radio or television broadcasts originating outside Canada.
What has changed between the original wording in Bill C-51 and this particular motion, which we cannot support, is the fact that the Government, in its wisdom, in the final wording on the free trade agreement decided that it would offer preferential tax treatment to American advertisers, in the same manner as is currently available to Canadian advertisers in magazines. One might say that that is totally unrelated to the Bill that is before us. What is being set up here by way of Bill C-51 is a limitation and a prohibition on advertising in Canadian magazines of Canadian tobacco products beyond a certain date.

May 31, 1988
Tobacco Products
Presumably, entrepreneurial American advertisers and tobacconists who may see the possibility of moving into the Canadian market in the near future as a result of the trade agreement could very easily receive preferential tax treatment to advertise American tobacco products in American magazines which are also available for sale in Canada. That particular issue was discussed in detail in committee. In fact, it was determined in committee that we did not wish to permit a situation where American tobacconists and American advertisers could bypass our law by attempting to target the Canadian market. The unanimous view of the committee was thwarted specifically by Subsection (3). Basically, that subsection is stating that it is carte blanche for Americans to come in with American magazines loaded up and targeted toward Canadians, for which they will get preferential tax treatment, and attempt to capture a larger share of the Canadian market.
If we are entering into a free trade agreement, and if we are saying to Americans that they can come in and trade in any number of commodities, the same legislation that will apply to Canadian advertisers should also apply to any American advertisers who may want to target the Canadian market. By virtue of Subsection (3) the Minister is prohibiting any action that might be taken by the Canadian Government to stop the bootleg advertising that could occur and, in fact, could be attractive to Americans who, as a result of the trade agreement, are getting preferential tax treatment, and who will also see the opportunity to come in and capture a market share which would be stabilized as a result of the Canadian decision to prohibit advertising.
This is a glaring loophole for American tobacco companies and American advertisers which should not be allowed to pass by way of this particular amendment. That is why we cannot support the totality of Motion No. 1. We see that particular amendment as an attempt to permit American tobacco companies and American advertisers to launch an assault on the Canadian market with preferential tax treatment in the manner that is currently being disallowed for Canadian advertisers and Canadian tobacco companies. That is not acceptable.
Therefore, in relation to Motion No. 1, we strongly urge the Parliamentary Secretary, since the Minister has seen fit to be elsewhere, to prevail upon the Minister to pull this subsection which is an assault on the integrity of the Bill, and by way of specific amendments to ensure that American companies will not be able to exploit a situation which will flow from the adoption of this legislation, and that is specifically as it relates to the rights of Americans to advertise American products targeting Canadian markets.
The Hon. Member is shaking her head. Perhaps she did not have the opportunity to read the position paper put forward by the Law and Government Division representative, Mr. James R. Robertson. He prepared a paper for the committee. It was his view that if preferential tax treatment were offered under the free trade agreement, there would be the potential of a threat from American advertisers who, in an indirect way,
attempted to get their message across to the Canadian marketplace.
Many people in my home town of Hamilton watch CHCH television, but many people also flick the television to U.S. channels and are very subject to the onslaught of U.S. advertising. In the spirit of the so-called trade agreement, surely the Minister should make provisions to cut this off at the pass and ensure that entrepreneurial tobacco companies will not be using border crossings, border magazines, and border broadcasts as a way to indirectly target the Canadian market-place. That is why this amendment cannot go through. It specifically prohibits the Canadian Government from taking action against these advertisers.
I was one who fought in committee to specifically change the wording so that instead of just referring to advertising in Canada, it would say "no person", so that a company in New York could not be hired to direct an advertising campaign out of the United States into the very populous market-place of southwestern Ontario, a place which is very subject to the onslaught of American advertisers. Unfortunately, the concerns of the committee have been watered down and in fact nullifed by this particular motion. That motion obviously cannot pass.
With respect to Motion No. 2, given that the Minister has taken much longer than had been anticipated in bringing Bill C-51 forward for final reading, the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood realized that to move an amendment which would affect health signs posted before July 1 at this point would be rather moot. By the time the Bill gets Royal Assent, July 1, 1988, will obviously have passed and the Minister may want to look at changing that date or in some way modifying that. I find that at this point, Motion No. 2 is almost redundant, given that the Minister was so long in bringing the Bill forward.
Motions Nos. 3 and 4 obviously deal with grandfathering. The Minister did make a compromise which was a response to sports organizations and other cultural organizations that were concerned about the possibility of getting alternate funding. The motions that have been moved by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) basically cut in half and then in quarter the time allowed for grandfathering of sponsorship items. This reflects the recognition that sponsoring groups will have to phase out tobacco funding. These motions accelerate the process.
The Minister's own motion calls for a grandfathering clause which would permit unto infinity current funding levels for sports and cultural events that already exist. The amendment suggests that that be pared down by first one-half and then one-quarter. We think that is a good compromise, based on the concerns many people have, concerns which were very validly expressed.

Mr. Speaker, 1 appreciate the opportunity to say a few words about the matter of the possibility that sponsorship of events, I think particularly here of sporting events, will be allowed to continue. This question is of very great importance to Canadians. Our desire to discourage the young from smoking should, surely, be our
goal. The Government has failed to follow through on this. The amendments proposed, particularly Motion No. 7 by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) dealt with that. While smoking is still being taken up by young people these days, and one could expand on that at some length, older Canadians recognize the dangers of it and are giving it up. Men especially are giving up smoking in recognition of its dangers. But teenagers and children at incredibly tender ages are getting addicted to tobacco and are suffering all of its consequences.
We should be concerned for their well-being and their good health. We should be concerned about the cost to society and the cost to employers resulting from this habit if continued over the years. We must be concerned about the consequences to our health care system in caring for smokers. We have been told that we will have to make brutal choices. Someone's addiction to tobacco will lead to discrimination against such a person obtaining medical treatment. What is the point, given what this person has done to himself or herself over many years, in providing medical care to such an individual. There in a few thoughts are some of the dangers. Surely we have a responsibility and the Government of Canada has a responsibility to limit the encouragement of smoking in society.
Soon after I was elected I became aware of the problem, serving as critic in the area of fitness and amateur sport. The Minister recognized the challenge. It was not an easy one with Macdonald Inc. having become involved in sponsorship of events, especially ski-jumping. It was not easy to tell the association and the athletes who were depending on the money about a ban. I attended a dinner in Thunder Bay. It was clear that very soon after the Minister imposed his ban, a prospective ban at some future date, the lobbying came from the association and local people. I remember a speech made by representatives of Macdonald Inc. left no doubt about their dislike of the ban, about their desire to continue sponsorship and to have the Macdonald name advertised.
The Government decided to cave in to that kind of pressure and allowed the Macdonald name to remain incorporated in one event or another. It may be one thing to have tobacco advertising for adults and one thing to have it for professional sports, if you will, but to see tobacco advertising for amateur sporting events involving young people surely should not be allowed. If the Government has caved in on this, we have just one more area of weakness in Bill C-51 that we are debating at report stage today.
Motion No. 7 moved by the Hon. Member for Broadview- Greenwood will put back in the Bill:
"6. No person shall employ the brand name or a trade mark of a tobacco product in any representation made to the public for the purpose of acknowledging financial or other support provided by a manufacturer or
May 31, 1988

importer of tobacco products for an activity, event, publication or broadcast."
Surely the financial need can be met by reputable employers-and one can use that kind of a phrase when there are companies whose businesses lead to disease and death, but there must be companies whose business is conducive to a good life, long life, good health et cetera who have the means to come up with resources. One might say that some of the taxes raised from tobacco companies might be directed to fitness and amateur sport if one has to find resources through tax means, but let us get tobacco advertising removed and let us use this amendment and Motion No. 9 which would return to the Bill the second reading date as the cut-off point for sponsorship. These amendments go in the right direction.
I urge my colleagues, if they have any kind of concern at all, to have effective legislation for the good health of young people and if they have any kind of concern for employers who want to have healthy employees and if they have any kind of consent for themselves as taxpayers and the Canadian health care system, to pass these amendments, and not give them the kind of defeat I fear the Government will give.

Mr. Speaker, this is one time when I have to disagree with the position taken by the New Democratic Party. I am completely baffled as to the New Democrats' rationale. We just had a Member who moved a grandfathering clause in recognition of sporting events, not wholly grandfathering but partially grandfathering, namely, the amendment moved by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow).
Presumably the grandfathering amendment is recognizing that sports organizations will need some time to make transitional funding. But now we have another amendment that says that even though we have said in one amendment that will grandfather sponsorships, we want the sponsorships grandfathered with no brand name. We have already stated, and we have heard time and again in committee, that tobacco companies do not sponsor because they happen to be magnanimous and wonderful people, they sponsor because they want to advertise. If you endorse, which presumably you have in part by accepting an amendment which would grandfather sponsorships, you cannot realistically argue from both sides of your mouth, which is now being attempted. Either you ban grandfathering altogether or you allow grandfathering to continue in a limited or in a reduced way.
The motion moved on brand names is completely unworkable. If anyone has read the legislation, he or she will know that if du Maurier wants to run the du Maurier Special, instead of using the tobacco company name all it needs to do is incorporate a second company called du Maurier. The loophole to get around whatever legislation is brought forward is so wide, why not say: "We are grandfathering. We will continue with the current system for a prescribed period of time, in fact, reducing by half the amount of sponsorship dollars available". You cannot, Mr. Speaker, state on the one hand that you want
Tobacco Products
to grandfather, which is what the New Democrats have done with the amendment just moved by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North, yet expect the grandfathering to occur with no brand name.
I know the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Epp) has received correspondence, as have all Members, from sporting and cultural organizations. Presumably that is why he said what he did about the issue of funding, that he was happy that some kind of compromise had been reached even though it was not exactly what he wanted. Well, if the Darts Federation, for example, is not allowed to have a sponsor which uses a brand name, obviously the companies are not going to sponsor them.
These contracts are not written in stone. You either grandfather fully or partially or not at all. You cannot say you are going to do it and send a letter out to all the sporting organizations to that effect and then move an amendment two minutes later saying you do not want people using their brand name. Obviously the grandfathering is phoney. If you grandfather, you have to say that for a given period of time we are going to permit continued sponsorship based on a cut-back of 50 per cent of the funding available to sports organizations. That is the intent of the amendment. We will not have grandfathering at 1987 financial levels, but we will have grandfathering which will cut in half the amount of money available in 1987.
If you do have grandfathering you cannot move an amendment saying that brand names shall not be used because, first, it is so easy for a company to get around that. All they have to do is incorporate under the name du Maurier Special. Second, if they are not allowed to put their brand name forward, presumably they are not going to sponsor. The reason we grandfathered the sponsorship was in recognition of the fact it will take time for these sports and cultural organizations to get other funding. However, if we then say no brand name can be used the companies will yank their sponsorship tomorrow, and you are not responding to the need that was supposedly the reason for the grandfathering. Motion No. 7 is a total contradiction of Motion No. 3 and Motion No. 4. They are inconsistent, so we cannot support Motion No. 7.
Motion No. 8 and Motion No. 9 clarify the level of sponsorship and the cut-off point and also set out some guidelines with respect to grandfathering. They are supportable, but we cannot support Motion No. 7 which vitiates Motions. Nos. 3 and 4. I do not understand the NDP. If you do not want to grandfather at all, say so. That is legitimate. But if you do, do not say you are going to do it without the brand or trade name because it does not work.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciated listening to the comments of the Hon. Member regarding what appears to be a conflicting set of motions. Perhaps I could respond by simply saying this. Motion No. 7 is

Tobacco Products
one of the toughest of this set of amendments. The effort here is more than symbolic. The Hon. Member for Broadview- Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) is simply trying to say, to the young people particularly, let us not have a major cultural or sporting event supported up front by tobacco companies. I do not think there is anything mysterious about that.
Other Members are saying the reality is that grandfathering is required. Contracts have been signed and so on. That needs to be recognized, but we have to remember that the Hon. Member has a particularly strong view on this issue. It is perhaps one of the strongest in the House. She is simply saying: "Let us send a very clear signal to everyone that we find it abhorrent that young people participating in recreational or athletic activities are being continuously reminded that the reason it is being held is because of a tobacco company".
In one way we have always appreciated the financial endorsement, but I find it somewhat puzzling as a father with two young sons involved in a variety of sporting events because I suspect they are wondering whether or not they should smoke. They see their peers smoking. They see the big tobacco companies of the western world advocating that if you ski well or surf well or do whatever well and have a cigarette at the end, that makes perfect sense. Of course it is totally illogical that anyone at all interested in athletics or sporting events would be a regular smoker. That is absolute folly. Any suggestion that this would be good for my two sons I find abhorrent. Anyone trying to encourage my two sons to participate in smoking or chewing tobacco or whatever else, I find to be repugnant. I do not think we ought to be encouraging that at all. We should be doing the contrary and discouraging it. I suspect, as a very famous football player yourself, Mr. Speaker, you know that to play football, the way you did and the way we like to see our teams play football we do not want people smoking a package of cigarettes at the end of the game or chewing a wad of Copenhagen or whatever.
A clause that says no person shall employ the brand name or trade mark of a tobacco product in any representation made to the public for the purpose of acknowledging financial or other support provided by a manufacturer or importer of tobacco products for an activity, event, publication or broadcast to me makes perfect sense. It is a tough position to take. I suspect the tobacco companies and importers would not like this amendment. I appreciate why from the traditional and obvious business point of view. However, for the best interests of our society, particularly our young people who are susceptible to both direct and indirect forms of advertising, an enthusiastic endorsement of this amendment would be the most we could do as parliamentarians to say that we want to do whatever possible to encourage our young people particularly not to smoke.

Mr. Speaker, I want to address this group of amendments and clear up an apparent misunderstanding on the part of the Hon. Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps). Motion No. 7 is the
motion we want. That says sponsorship cannot be used for advertising. No person shall employ the brand name or trade mark of a tobacco product in any representation made to the public for acknowledging financial or other support. We want to get rid of it because we know that so long as sponsorship is allowed, the opportunity will be taken by the cigarette companies to use that for advertising purposes. However, given all the pressure put on the Government and the fact it is caving in, we are not so sure Motion No. 7 will go through. If not, then we would like Motion No. 9. That would limit the sponsorship for contracts which have come in before April 30, 1987, at the time the Bill was introduced. We would at least have some limitation on these sponsorships. If we do not go the way I would like us to go, and that is get rid of them completely, let us at least limit them to the ones already in place and not encourage the tobacco companies to enter into new contracts for sponsorship and shift their advertising dollars into sponsorship and get their advertising that way. It is very important that we get that one passed.
Motion No. 8 would clarify the conditions under which tobacco sponsorship may continue. That is the Minister's motion and part of his weaker approach to say we are not going to get rid of it completely, we will allow some of it, and it simply clarifies the conditions. We would much prefer to get the stronger one.
Motion No. 10 would give the Government the right to prescribe the format and conditions of acknowledgement of sponsorship. Again, we would rather get rid of the sponsorship completely but if it is going to be there, let us have it clearly defined by regulation so that the companies cannot get around the law by having sponsorships and then having great massive kinds of acknowledgments. They are going to be allowed to acknowledge? How big is the sign going to be on which they can acknowledge their sponsorship? If the Government is going to capitulate and allow some sponsorship, let us at least define the terms of it very carefully.
Therefore, there is a logic to these, Mr. Speaker. They are not contradictory. We have an order of priorities and would like to get the best we can out of the Government.

subsubtopic: HOCKEY NIGHT IN CANADA TELEVISION CONTRACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we learned this morning that the CBC may not be broadcasting Hockey Night in Canada this coming season. Instead, reports indicate, the CTV network will take over this 55-year tradition which began with Foster Hewitt broadcasting on radio in 1933.
Foster is no longer with us, but fully two generations of Canadians-especially those in northern and remote parts of Canada-will remember how Hockey Night in Canada provided an opportunity for families, friends, and neighbours in many an isolated village or reserve to get together to enjoy watching a truly Canadian event.
If the CBC cancels Hockey Night in Canada, those same Canadians will also remember this Government. They will
May 31, 1988

remember that the Mulroney Conservatives promised to reach out to the regions of Canada when they sought office in 1984. Instead, the Government has cut back its support of the CBC financially, and more recently it has tried to scuttle the CBC all-news network.
It is unfair that Canadians who cannot afford the expensive cable services of northern Canada, or who do not even have access to cable, may no longer receive a most enjoyable sports program on the only network available in many communities.
I and my New Democratic colleagues call upon the Government to guarantee that the CBC will continue to broadcast Hockey Night in Canada. Foster Hewitt would, I am sure, echo those sentiments.

Mr. Speaker, on April 13 the CBC's The Journal broadcast one of the most grossly biased programs ever seen on the subject of abortion. The entire program consisted of interviews only with those who favour abortion on demand.
The name of the people on the panel were Jeannie MacPher-son and Joan Wright, pro-abortion women counsellors; Phyllis Bowman, British pro-life activist; Vivianne Nathanson, proabortion member of the British Medical Association; Shiela Martin, pro-abortion Professor of Law, University of Calgary; and David Roy, pro-abortion member of the Centre for Bioethics in Montreal.
Each one of them made it clear that they do not support the rights of the unborn children from the moment of conception.
The CBC has no right at all to impose its own view of morality on the Canadian public. This program is a clear violation of its mandate to produce balanced programming.
I call upon the CRTC to censor the CBC by insisting that the CBC live up to its mandate for balanced programming, to include both sides of an issue, and not just the CBC's bias.

HOSPICE PALLIATIVE CARE SOCIETY OF EASTERN NOVA SCOTIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to bring to the attention of the House the efforts of the Hospice Palliative Care Society of eastern Nova Scotia. This group of dedicated volunteers work to help enrich the quality of life for the terminally ill in Cape Breton. They
have dedicated this week as the annual Hospice Palliative Care Week.
This service is valuable to the residents of eastern Nova Scotia. It is the first and only comprehensive program for terminally ill patients and their families. It is a non-profit group which operates in both the home and the hospitals to provide care and compassion to those who have no hope for a cure.
The Society has a medical component which strives to give patients a pain-free existence for their remaining days. The Society also acts as a support system for the families involved. It works with the families to promote a peaceful death of the patient in the home environment. Although the Society has no religious affiliation, pastoral care is provided.
I salute all those involved in this compassionate program and wish them success in this most difficult endeavour.

UNITED NATIONS SPECIAL SESSION ON DISARMAMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like all Canadians I am my colleagues welcome the current superpower summit in Moscow between President Reagan and General-Secretary Gorbachev. In particular we welcome the growing understanding and co-operation this and previous summits encourage between the superpowers, particularly in the area of meaningful reductions in the nuclear arsenals of the two countries.

May 31, 1988
While we welcome these discussions we must also keep in mind that equally important discussions are currently taking place at the Third United Nations Special Session on Disarmament. Unfortunately, UNSSOD III has not received the attention it deserves, particularly on the part of the Canadian Government, which has not adequately outlined the positions it plans to take at the special session on such critical disarmament issues as the modernization of nuclear weapons in Europe, limits on Cruise missile development and deployment, reductions in strategic nuclear forces, and the creation of an international verification regime.
These and other disarmament issues are as critical to Canada's security as they are to the security of the superpowers. I call on the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) to tell the House and the Canadian people where his Government stands on these important issues. A ministerial statement prior to the Minister's address to the UN would be a welcome gesture.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to commend the strength of the Government's commitment to recognize multiculturalism as a central feature of our identity.
Last December the Government tabled the historic new Multiculturalism Act, Bill C-93. Even before the Bill becomes law, the Government is reinforcing the policies and the ideals of the multiculturalism policy of Canada.
Over five years $192 million has been added to the annual multiculturalism budget, which means it will rise to $42.2 million by 1991-92. That is 80 per cent more than was spent in 1986-87.
This is not tokenism or half-hearted support. This is action. It is action that will extend this Government's priorities of social justice and national harmony into every segment of our society.
The new directions announced yesterday by the Minister of State for Multiculturalism (Mr. Weiner) will strengthen race relation initiatives, and improve understanding among our many different cultures. They will help preserve and enhance our multicultural heritage. They will ensure equality of opportunity for all Canadians.
These new funds and the leadership provided by the Government will help make that ideal a deeply felt reality.

END OF INDUSTRIAL AND REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, tomorrow marks the end of the Industrial and Regional Development Program that has served the Province of Quebec so well in recent years. We know that the program ends tomorrow and that no other program to replace it has been announced by the Minister responsible. I feel that for the last six months, the Minister has been fooling around on a replacement program and Quebec industrialists and the various industrial commissioners are extremely concerned. We know that the Association of Industrial Commissioners made representations to the Member for Langelier (Mr. Cote) and when he was Minister, he did nothing because he was too busy with other matters and now the present Minister has not bothered with a replacement for IRDP either.
As a result, in view of the impact this program has in diversifying the industrial base of many regions, Quebec is being left behind as the poor relation in regional economic development and I trust that in the coming weeks, the Minister will finally bring forward a program that will meet the aspirations of Quebec companies and the needs of the Quebec economy as well as of some regions of Ontario.
We know that a byelection is to be held in Lac-Saint-Jean. I suppose that the Minister will try to buy his way and save the skin of the Secretary of State with a few million dollars from Regional Industrial Expansion. But I think now is the time to announce the program to replace IRDP which has served us so well and several regions will be neglected because of the Minister's negligence.

subtopic: DUMPING OF INDUSTRIAL WASTES IN GREAT LAKES
DUMPING OF INDUSTRIAL WASTES IN GREAT LAKES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, poisoned Ontario lake water has helped to kill off thousands of beluga whales in the St. Lawrence River estuary.
Last weekend a ship called the Beluga was sailed by Greenpeace to Toronto to remind us about the poisons in the same lake water that we drink.
Canadian and American corporations dump industrial wastes into our lake system that can cause cancer, damage our nervous systems, and damage our immune systems. For years the federal Government has known this and done nothing to stop it.
The federal Government is responsible, with the United States, for the Great Lakes water. Why is it neglecting its responsibility and allowing the fish, the whales, and us to be poisoned?
As well as taking action to stop the polluters and punish them if necessary, the federal Government must fund new water treatment systems. Our present water treatment systems were not built to remove poisons such as these.
The federal Government must employ Canadian men and women to design, make, install, and operate modern water treatment equipment that will give us clean, safe water to drink.

The Bible states: "The Lord gave her conception". From that moment on, life is God's responsibility and not Parliament's. The decision of the Supreme Court has given Parliament the opportunity to show that Canada fears and respects God.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to express my concern for Canada's tourism industry in light of the ever widening gap between the price of gasoline in Canada and the price of gasoline in the United States as a result of the Government's taxation policies. Because of the sales tax and the excise tax increases put in place by this Conservative Government, the difference between the price of gas in Canada and in the United States has now reached alarming proportions.
I regret to say that the price of all grades of gasoline is now, on average, 60 per cent more expensive in Canada than in the U.S., and that is taking the exchange rate into account. In September of 1984, at the time of the last federal election, the difference in price was only 22.1 per cent.
The Conservative Government, as always, refuses to recognize the negative effect this price differential is having on the tourism industry in Canada. When we consider that 70 per cent of tourism travel coming from the U.S. to Canada is by automobile, the effect is surely great. The Conservative Government is threatening to make Canada's tourism industry uncompetitive. I therefore call upon the Government to review its taxation policy as it affects tourism.

CHINOOK TAGGING PROGRAM-SIZE AND COST OF TAGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I recently met with fishers from Vancouver Island about confusion in the new one-dollar chinook tagging program. Costing the Government 63 cents a piece, flown in from Brazil, landed in Winnipeg instead of Vancouver, the tags are too small to fit around the tails of the chinook which are headed after being caught. Attaching the tags through the fish as suggested by fisheries officials will reduce the grade of the fish and lower the price given for the salmon.
When the plan was first introduced, officials indicated the tags would be supplied free of charge to commercial fishers who would have paid at the end of the season for the tags used. Now the Government requires payment up front. Many trollers are hard pressed to come up with the money to purchase these tags.
Fishers will face fines for any untagged chinook landed. However, the Government has no plans to help them if they find themselves without the adequate number of tags once out on the grounds. They will be forced to head into port to purchase additional tags. Unless a solution is found we will see the off-loading of untagged Chinooks before the catch is landed.
There is still time before the season opens to rectify these problems and to ensure fishers are not penalized due to the Department of Fisheries' inability to introduce an efficient, effective, and acceptable tagging program.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I said, I will not be very long but there are two or three things I would like to say this afternoon.
The purpose of the Bill is to provide a legislative response to a national public health problem of substantial and present concern. It is intended to protect the health of Canadians in light of conclusive evidence implicating tobacco use and the incidence of numerous debilitating and fatal diseases. It is also intended to protect all Canadians, especially young Canadians, from inducement to use tobacco products and consequent dependence on them. A further aim is to enhance public awareness of the health hazards of tobacco use by ensuring the effective communication of pertinent information to consumers of tobacco products.
The proposed ban on all tobacco advertising and most tobacco promotion is part of a wide-ranging anti-smoking policy that includes education measures, restrictions on public and workplace smoking, and financial assistance to tobacco farmers who wish to convert to alternative economic activity. This concerted government effort is aimed at promoting and eventually achieving a smoke-free society. These strong measures are an essential response to the pervasiveness of a man-made health problem which has reached epidemic proportions world-wide.
The most conspicuous triumphs of modern preventive medicine have concerned the control of infectious diseases, including smallpox, typhoid and polio. The most conspicuous failure has been in the area of tobacco-related illnesses, the leading public health concern of our time. Each year in Canada alone 35,000 middle-aged and older people die prematurely of tobacco-related illnesses, and thousands more suffer from tobaeCo-related chronic disabilities. These diseases,
May 31, 1988

which cause one out of every six deaths in Canada, can be prevented. However, a new vaccine is not the answer. The solution has to come from society as a whole and our collective willingness to strip tobacco of its falsely alluring image.
That really is the essence of the Bill, so I am not going into its various details again. However, I received one piece of additional information which will possibly make the argument one more time to those who might be skeptical or those who say the tobacco industry and its advertising arm are not interested in inducing young Canadians to smoke. I have in my hand Maclean's magazine of May 30, 1988, and I do not think I can get any more current than that. In that magazine there is an ad for pipe tobacco with a clip-out coupon. The ad in this national news magazine says:
New Amphora Cherry Cavendish. It's cool, smooth and easy-smoking. For a
free pouch of Amphora Cherry, send the label from your regular tobacco or
cigarette brand with this coupon to Delpro,-
It then gives the address. I had one of the young people who work with me call that company today at noon. They were asked what is required. They said, "Send a note with your name, address and phone number, and your name will go into a computer bank so we can send you our tobacco newsletter. Tell us which brand you smoke and we will send you your free pouch of pipe tobacco". There is no cost, there are no questions, and there was no reference to age. Anyone who can dial a number or fill out the coupon can do it.
You might say that most young Canadians might not want their first experience with tobacco to be pipe tobacco. However, the tobacco industry from day one has wanted to attract more people to their products so they could sell more of them. Anyone who denies that flies in the face of every piece of evidence. I say that in a country where we spend so much time protecting health, where we look for cancer cures and cures for heart disease, lung disease, and try to develop a better quality of life, it is time for this Parliament to speak.
It is a testimony to the tobacco industry that it is the only industry, with the exception of the 1908 law, with no restrictions on it by law. You tell me whether you can buy any consumer product on which there are not some restrictions. Tobacco has escaped.
People say, what about freedom of speech? The Charter of Rights and Freedoms is not a charter for companies, it is a charter for individual Canadians. Some people say there will be a challenge to this Bill with respect to the right to advertise. I say, "Challenge us. Challenge the Parliament of Canada. Challenge Canadians. At the same time, explain why you want to protect an industry responsible for more self-induced illness and death than any other in Canada today". Those are pretty strong words, but I mean them, not only as an individual but as Minister of National Health and Welfare.
The time has come where Ministers responsible for health cannot simply utter nice, comforting words about health. Action has to be taken. Therefore, I call on this Parliament to take that action. I also call on the other place to prove that it

Section 2(b) of the new Charter of Rights and Freedoms guarantees "freedom of thought, belief, opinion and expression." Three Provincial Courts of Appeal have recognized that this guarantee extends to advertising (Manitoba, Quebec, and Alberta) and a fourth has confirmed that the guarantee protects all forms of expression (Ontario). view to take up the cudgel with respect to this legislation, but I am annoyed by it because I think that it not only offends the Charter of Rights and the values I believe in, such as freedom of speech but, in addition, I think it is socially useless legislation.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the Hon. Member for Cambridge (Mr. Speyer) on the position he has taken. I have listened to his speech very carefully and although I am a non-smoker myself and opposed to smoking, I agree with him that it would be more intellectually honest to outlaw smoking than to prohibit the right to advertise.
I agree with him that the position the Government is taking is directly contrary to the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. I realize it was not easy for the Hon. Member to make his speech. As one Member of Parliament, I appreciate the position he has taken and the trouble and courage he took to make his speech.
I have one question for the Hon. Member. Concerning statistics on whether advertising does encourage smoking, could he tell us what he has found in his research in that regard?

Mr. Speaker, first, may I thank the Hon. Member for the very generous comments he has given me. I am most appreciative.
With respect to answering the Member's question, it seems to me that the pivotal point with respect to this legislation is whether or not it will in any way reduce smoking. We asked every witness about statistics in other countries on the effectiveness of advertising to reduce smoking. It was absolutely clear to me on the evidence that I heard that there is nothing to justify that. Not only am I buoyed in terms of the evidence I heard but I do not believe the Government believes it. Why would you have a cabinet document which said it was only being done for symbolic reasons? Symbolic reasons are not bad reasons, Mr. Speaker. It may be you want to show that there is some sense of moral opprobrium against smoking. Being symbolic is necessarily not legitimate, but there is absolutely no doubt in my mind that the statistics to not warrant the conclusion that this legislation will reduce smoking by one cigarette.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for my colleague. He is opposed to this legislation because he feels and said that advertising meant to promote smoking is ineffective and does not have any impact on whether people smoke or not. Why does he think that tobacco companies spend all the money they do on advertising if it is not to encourage people to smoke?
Related to that, the Member indicated he is opposing this legislation because of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. What about the right to health? What about the right of the young person who will be induced to take up the habit of
May 31, 1988

smoking as a result of advertising? What about that young person's right to health? What about the right of the public not to have commercial enterprises promoting a habit detrimental to health which costs the public purse because people develop diseases from smoking? What about the right of families to be free of suffering? What about the 35,000 people who die as a result of diseases caused by tobacco?

I thank the Hon. Member for his question, Mr. Speaker. It is a perfectly reasonable one. The essence of what my friend is saying goes to smoking itself.
I listened to him articulate with some degree of force all the problems of smoking with respect to health and emotional concerns. As a result of that, he arrived at the essence of the question which is whether we should ban smoking itself. On the one hand, how can one say we are going to allow smoking and yet, on the other hand, say we will not allow the advertising of a product which is legal? That concerns me. If we were talking about a product that is illegal such as cocaine, that is different.
I acknowledge there are limits on speech. For example, defamation, libel and slander are limits on speech. There have to be some limits on speech. When you take a broad blanket and say there will be no advertising whatever with respect to a product I believe that you are intruding on a person's right to make a decision. Why doesn't the Hon. Member have the courage to sponsor a Bill to prohibit smoking? That is the point. It is not the advertising but the smoking itself. In brief response-
Why do the companies advertise?
May I be permitted to answer the Hon. Member's question?
Why do the companies advertise?

I would like to address that. There is no doubt, tobacco companies want to sell cigarettes. That is why they advertise. The evidence that persuaded me is that of market share. If the Hon. Member took a look at the eastern European bloc countries where there is really no advertising, the incidence of smoking is higher than we have here. If you take a look at what has happened in some Scandinavian countries, the incidence of smoking has not in any way decreased. Those countries have done something symbolic, which is what the Minister and the Government are trying to do. I do not agree to that. If we want to be courageous we should pass a ban on smoking itself, not the advertising of it.

Mr. Speaker, I am very glad to have the opportunity today to address Bill C-51 and to speak in favour of albeit a very small step in the battle against tobacco addiction in this country. The short title of the Bill is the Tobacco Products Control Act, but I must say the short title is at variance with the long title. This is not really a tobacco products control Bill, it is a Bill of limited application.
Tobacco Products
I believe it is of somewhat limited usefulness in the continuing struggle against tobacco addiction.
Nevertheless, a small step though this Bill will be, it is one that I and my Party support and a step that I believe all Members in this House should support. Bill C-51 has received the almost unanimous endorsement of health organizations in this country from the great national federations down to local clinics. It is a Bill that has received considerable public support. It has been the subject of a very targeted campaign against its passage by the smoking and tobacco products lobby but I believe there is no doubt that it is supported.
However, this sort of legislation must be seen in the context of other legislation that will be brought in, something I will return to later. What we have after all in the case-

As they say in French: le tabagisme est un fleau. It is indeed a plague that annually takes the lives of 35,000 fellow citizens.

That means that with some 30,000 to 32,000 people dying from smoking-related cancers and some 3,000 people dying from the effects of passive or side-stream smoking we have a loss in terms of the lives of Canadians that we cannot permit to continue.
The passive smoking problem is well-documented, much discussed and I will not comment on it in depth. However, I do believe the attention given to its effect is a clear indication that the social acceptability of smoking is declining. I believe that of course it must continue to decline and that any measure this House takes, even though it be seen by some as symbolic, is worth taking. I believe we will see a further decline in the social acceptability of smoking over the next few years. I believe it will soon come to be acknowledged that smoking in the presence, for example, of a child is a form of child abuse. I believe that society will recognize that smoking in the presence of one who does not desire to have the air polluted is indeed a form of assault. I believe that when it comes to workplace considerations, it can already be proven to be a civil tort if such a case were launched.
The Hon. Member for Cambridge (Mr. Speyer), who is perhaps now enjoying a coffee and cigarette, talked about free speech. He is a Member with enough experience and intellect, indeed he showed it in his speech, to recognize there are indeed limitations on the so-called freedom of speech in a free society. Any freedom exercised to the ultimate is mere libertinage. Any freedom pressed to its limits ends of course in the oppression of others. That is what happens on a daily, even hourly, basis, and even in these parliamentary precincts.
Let me talk about some of the limits on the concept of freedom of speech, limits which have come about in democratic societies as a response to the problems and antagonisms caused by licence instead of liberty in the exercise of free

May 31, 1988
Tobacco Products
speech. So it is we have laws against incitement to hatred. We have laws against sedition. As the Hon. Member for Cambridge mentioned, we have laws against slander, libel, and defamation of character. We also have laws against conspiracy. We have laws against the publication of hate propaganda. We have laws against the promulgation of pornography, which so many of us see these days as being a little more than hate propaganda directed against women and children.
I have to say that the Hon. Member for Cambridge, in talking about tobacco as a legal product, is not conducting an adequate historical analysis before applying that judgment. I believe tobacco's legality today is nothing more than an accident. It is a result of the fact that tobacco smoking was widespread in this country before we realized and scientifically demonstrated the degree to which tobacco consumption affected health.
I see the legality of smoking as being nothing more than an historical accident. Yet I will concede that were we to talk of but a moment in time, the Hon. Member's arguments would have more credibility than in fact they do. In judging time by a moment we ignore the expanse of history. We ignore the actual process in society of which this Bill is but a part.
Another point that I must take up is the mention of choice in the consumption of tobacco. The fact is that talking of people choosing to smoke or choosing not to smoke ignores the very persuasive evidence that tobacco is an addictive narcotic. The fact that a person continues to smoke, and I think as a non-smoker this is something I have to remind myself of continually, does not necessarily reflect a choice. It reflects the fact that many people are addicted to the product. I think it is incumbent upon us as a society to be gentle with people but tough on behaviour. Therefore, as individuals we have to raise with those who offend, when they do so against the norms of those of us who wish to have breathable air, a defence not only of our civil liberty to breathable air but also our health.
As an asthmatic, I of course have a very strong personal stake in legislation, regulation, consensus or agreement which reduces the amount of smoke I am forced to inhale. Therefore, I have to support Bill C-51 on that ground.
In conclusion, I would like again to pick up the point I was making earlier about the place of this Bill in a continuum or ensemble of measures designed to reduce smoking. It cannot be seen as legislation that stands on its own. Indeed, I believe the Hon. Minister never intended this Bill should stand on its own but saw it as part of a sequence. In order to demonstrate that point I would like to quote from page 24:21 of the legislative committee hearing on Bill C-51 on January 25, 1988:
In an additional effort to improve Canada's health-oriented policy on tobacco, further amendments will be introduced in order to update the Tobacco Restraint Act, which has made it illegal since 1908 to sell tobacco products to persons under the age of 16. At the report stage-and we have checked this with our lawyers and I would like to do it today but I cannot do it because of the scope of the bill-the government will seek the consent of
Parliament to repeal the Tobacco Restraint Act and incorporate such
provisions, updated so as to be relevant to the 1980s and 1990s, into Bill C-51.
It seems to me that that objective has fallen somewhat by the wayside, but I believe the intent of the Minister was very clear. While I, too, hold the value of intellectual honesty which the Hon. Member propounds, I have to ask: Does adherence to that value justify the sacrifice in lives and health which we as a society are allowing to continue? It is in that context that I believe Bill C-51 is worth-while, must be supported, and should pass.
