Mr. Speaker, I will not take long but I wish to comment on what the Hon. Member had to say because in his last few words he put the issue extraordinarily well and clearly. I also want to pick up on some of the comments made by the Hon. Member for Cambridge (Mr. Speyer).
As a reformed sinner, with respect to smoking at least, I support the main thrust of this Bill, namely to reduce smoking. Used smoke now bothers me as well as other people, and I support the Minister in his attempt to promote our health and welfare and cause all of us to think twice about smoking. He is taking a direction that he and other Members of this House believe is right and appropriate, and generally I admire his advice, his integrity and great ability so much that I would automatically vote with the Minister. At the moment, however, what I cannot support is a complete ban on advertising of what is in fact at the moment, by historic chance or not, a legal and freely available product.
We are, I think, taking chances with our important concept of freedom of expression, but we may not accomplish our objectives, which is exactly what the previous speaker said. That is the trade-off in this debate. I think there are other ways to accomplish those objectives without jeopardizing the concept which, to me, is fundamental-the freedom of expression.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the Hon. Member for his very kind words in relation to my speech. I believe that if we were all to approach this legislation with the measure of thought which the Hon. Member for Guelph (Mr. Winegard) has obviously brought to it, it would make for a very good debate.
I think many of us would like to have much more time to debate the principle of this Bill. I am still convinced of the correctness of my point. I am sure that those who feel afflicted by this legislation will seek a judgment in the courts regarding the applicability of the free speech provisions of the Charter of Rights to the commercial communication which, of course, the advertisers of tobacco would like to carry on unimpaired and unimpeded.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to ask my colleague a question with regard to this legislation. It is basically the same question which I asked my colleague on the other side of the House a few minutes ago. What is the impact of the advertising which tobacco companies finance? Does the Hon. Member agree with Members on the other side of the House who seem to say that tobacco companies spend all this money advertising cigarettes without this advertising having any impact on people's behaviour? Does he really think that tobacco companies are stupid enough to waste their money in that way?

Mr. Speaker, I, too, cannot believe that these vast sums are spent without the idea of creating or persuading new smokers. Surely the fact is that they are spent in efforts to reinforce a climate of acceptability of smoking. Indeed, they are spent as well to get people to switch brands, but the overall message of the advertising campaigns of the industry is to try to ensure that smoking remains socially acceptable.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to speak on what I think is an historic day, not only for Canada in terms of health measures and the improvement of the health of
Tobacco Products
Canadians, but an historic day for Parliament and its processes. There is an opportunity for private Members to vote in accordance with their own research and individual judgments and, equally important, for private Members to reflect on the health and well-being of all Canadians.
I have only a few moments to take on a couple of the arguments which I have heard in opposition to this legislation which I think need be addressed. First is the notion of freedom. There is the argument that I have the freedom to smoke, that it may be bad for me, but that somehow I have the fundamental right to smoke.
The only way smokers can claim that they have the right and freedom to smoke is if they never breathe out. People who breathe into other people's air are contaminators. Research for more than four decades in 50 countries has clearly demonstrated that smoking tobacco is a health hazard.
It is also curiously interesting that those persons who would argue on the other side of the issue do not take the position that smoking is harmful.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank all Members of the House for the courtesy they have just

May 31, 1988
Tobacco Products
extended. As soon as I have finished speaking every Member will want to vote on the Bill anyway.
There have been comments circulating with respect to the amount of tax dollars the Government of Canada receives from the tobacco industry. There has been a comment circulating throughout the duration of this debate trying to convince us that if we cut off or curtail tobacco advertising and, by implication, its sales, there would be a negative impact on the Treasury of the federal Government. The truth of the matter, Sir, which should be understood, is that if there were to be a cost recovery program for the use of tobacco the tax presently on tobacco would increase sevenfold.
If we take into account the clinic times, the hospital times, the deaths, the lost time from wages, all of which are related to sickness and illness from tobacco-
And fires.

And fires, as the Member for Oxford (Mr. Halliday) reminds me, if we took into account these costs, we would include in that formula seven times as much tax today to recover that cost to society. Even with 35,000 deaths per year directly related to smoking, and over 3,000 deaths from sidestream smoke, and the fact that the Treasury loses the billions of dollars it collects, there are still some who would argue that this noxious weed ought to be allowed to be sold freely to Canadians, as if this product could command the right to be advertised and promoted.
I want to go through the history of the tobacco industry. At one time its sales were primarily to males, promoting it as a male macho image. After the election of President Kennedy in the United States, who promoted the notion of a healthy America, the consumption of tobacco among males began to decrease significantly. The new thrust of advertising by the tobacco industry was for products like Virginia Slims. The message to females was: "You have come a long way, Baby". The theme was to capture a new market of female smokers.
More recently, when that market began to decline, it turned to young people. Now that it is being threatened by the activities taking place in the House of Commons, there has been a focus on Third World countries.
I have it from a very outstanding authority that Marlboro Country has gone to an African nation where their cigarettes are being promoted by people wearing white cowboy hats and white western uniforms while riding a white stallion and playing a banjo. They are given out to innocent people, cigarettes that have much higher tar content.
The World Health Organization will document the fact that they are moving their market increasingly into the Third World.
I do not believe those who suggest that tobacco advertising only shifts market brand. If that is true, why do Bell Canada
or Alberta Government Telephones advertise their products? Why is there advertising in monopoly markets? The fact is that advertising does increase consumption.
It was most amazing to hear the advertisers try to convince the committee that their advertising is ineffective. I have never before heard any group or organization tell a committee that it is ineffective. Yet the theme of their submission was that they were only shifting the brand share from one to another. Even if one were to believe that, it does not give reason or logic as to why monopolies advertise their products.
There are those who believe that our freedoms are most important, regardless of the damage they do to society. They pretend that somehow freedom exists in isolation. There is no freedom except that freedom which is measured by an equal and corresponding set of responsibilities.
We have the freedom of speech, but that does not allow us to go into a theatre and shout "fire", just to watch people run. We have freedom of mobility, but that does not allow us to drive at any speed and on any side of the road.
The notion that freedom means we can smoke and blow it into the atmosphere knowing full well that some 35,000 people per year die from tobacco and another 3,000 die from sidestream smoke, does not make sense or provide an appropriate argument.
More than four decades of research and more than 50 countries has led to the conclusion over and over again that tobacco is harmful to our health. It has demonstrated that in some individuals the addiction to tobacco is as strong as the addiction to heroin.
Not only do those who deny the importance of that kind of research question the credibility of the medical and research profession, they place extreme doubt on the science itself. Science has compelling evidence to make us ask as a society to do what this Parliament has the opportunity to do. Let us move in the right direction to protect the well-being and health of our citizens.
We hear the argument that this is a legal product and cannot be banned. I suggest that if it were possible, this product might be made illegal. However, one-third of Canadians are addicted to it and they probably curse Sir Walter Raleigh for it. If it was an easy procedure, I suggest it might even be made illegal. Yet everyone knows that it cannot be done because one-third of Canadians are addicted to tobacco and we must gradually eliminate its use.
Let us consider the question of illegality. We cannot advertise prescription drugs, explosives or poisons. There are many products that may be legal but cannot be advertised. There is no justification to say that the product cannot be used on that basis.
I want to thank the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) for the time he has gracefully given to me to make

Hear, hear!

speechtext:
Perhaps I can say, while I am on debate, that last week I was a little hasty in criticizing the Chair when perhaps we made a bit of a slip-up in terms of what was happening at about the same time. Perhaps the Liberals' interventions were related to the fact that they intended to have five people stand and did not do so at the appropriate time.
The motion in front of the House right now is a motion proposed by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Kamloops- Shuswap (Mr. Riis), asking that the Government, in conjunction with the provinces, establish a system whereby people who deposit money in financial institutions, and who are not covered by deposit insurance, be required to sign a waiver form to indicate that they are fully aware that their deposits are not insured, in the event that the institution goes bankrupt.
There have been a number of instances before the House where exactly that has happened. It happened in a number of cases where companies have played a bait and switch game with money that they have accepted from depositors. The depositors were led to believe that the money they were putting in was insured. They had been prudent in not putting more than 560,000 in a particular account with a particular institution. Yet, nonetheless, they found that they came up short, and in certain cases have lost all or a substantial amount of their life savings because of having put the money into an institution where it was not insured.
There is a very general problem that when there is insurance, people who put money on deposit, often some substantially in excess of $60,000, feel secure as a consequence of the insurance, and feel that as long as they spread their risk and do not put all the money into one institution, they do not have to worry and can go for absolutely the top rate of interest on their deposits without looking at the reputability or credibility of the institution.
Currently, steps are being taken to improve regulation of financial institutions. The Superintendent of Financial Institutions has received greater powers, new legislation, more staff, and has moved his locus of activities into the financial district in Toronto rather than being shut up here in Ottawa. Ottawa is the area that I represent and has many natural advantages, but perhaps it is a little distant from some of the things happening in financial markets.
The question of individual responsibility is a different question from that which I wish to deal with at the moment. I would not mind if a Government said that there should be a certain co-responsibility so that in the event of a financial failure the investor of over $10,000, bore a small proportion of the loss rather than being fully compensated, as is the case at the present time with insured deposits.
The present situation in which people put money into a trust company and believe that the money is an insured deposit, and

May 31, 1988
Financial Institutions
then find out that there was no such insurance, because through one device or another the money had been put into an uninsured form of investment, creates tragic results. The purpose of this motion is to attempt to ensure that that does not occur.
The background is as follows: between 1923 and the late 1970s there were few, if any, financial institutions in this country that failed. Therefore, people who put their money into deposits, particularly after the advent of mortgage insurance, felt relatively secure. The only exception was the Atlantic Acceptance affair in the 1960s. I recall looking at that situation when I was a financial journalist with the Financial Times. In the wake of that, there was the deposit insurance which provided great deal of security. At the beginning of the 1980s that financial insurance was substantially increased in value in the wake of the Seaway and Greymac affair in Ontario, in which I was also involved as an MPP.
An increasing number of financial institutions have got into trouble. That is a product of a number of causes. For example, globalization of finance, the advent of new financial institutions, the entry of Schedule B banks into Canada, the creation of small trust companies, the growth of the credit union movement, and at times some difficulties experienced by credit unions together with their rapid and important growth, the collapse of the Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank in western Canada, a collapse that the Government was prepared to bail out. It was an indication of the difficulties that financial institutions have, and also of the difficulties of regionally based banks. It will be some time before we again see the emergence of regionally based banks, except those that are supported by large foreign banks such as occurred with the Hongkong and Shanghai bank acquisition of the Bank of British Columbia.
Not only have there been collapses, but also near misses. In many cases, these are covered by deposit insurance. However, we must be aware of the fact that there are a substantial number of investment instruments which are not insured. At the same time, there is a broader proportion of Canadians who, for various reasons, have funds to insure. There is an increasing number of Canadians who put money into RRSPs because they are self-employed, or because they are moving from job to job and can take out their pension fund from one employer and put it into an RRSP without a tax penalty, self-administer it, or give it to the trust of a financial institution, in order that they can keep in touch with it. In fact, in many cases people are encouraged to do so by the employer whom they leave, or are forced to do so because the employer that they left was shut down and no longer in business.
There are many investors who may not be very sophisticated. There are people in the agricultural community who perhaps are selling off their family farm, or a portion of it, in order to get a pension fund and are putting money into various type of investments in order to provide themselves with a retirement income. Perhaps there are people who regrettably are forced out of a job because of economic adjustment, forced
by the trade agreement or other factors like that, who receive a sizeable amount of money and prudently put it into investments rather than spending it all. They find that they are looking at a combination of security and return, and one cannot always get both of those, yet people naively try to ensure that they get both.
The investment dealers hold about $3.5 billion in deposits from their clients and their customers, and the only insurance on that is what is called a national contingency fund. We know from the collapse of the Osier brokerage firm in Toronto that one such collapse can leave the fund empty. That contingency fund had about $20 million in credit and about $16 million in cash. The claims against it under the Osier bail-out exceeded, as I recall, the total amount it had on hand, and one particular client, in this case the Canadian Co-operative Credit Society, has been left holding the bag as a consequence of that.
There are in addition hundreds of companies across Canada that offer financial services and fund their operations by issuing debt instruments which are totally uninsured. I think we have to find some balance. For example, for a debt instrument in the form of a bond of a company in the market, it would perhaps be wrong to have to require a waiver. We do not want to have paperwork where it is not necessary, but for an institution which is accepting deposits or deposit-like investments from the public and putting them into short-term and medium-term investments of at least up to five years, the argument of my friend from Kamloops-Shuswap is that if that money is not going into an insured form, the investor should be required to sign a waiver.
If the investor signs a waiver and then later, if the company goes bankrupt and the deposit cannot be repaid, says the company should have told him or her, there is not much we can do except to say: "We are awfully sorry, but you were told". If a person were led to sign a waiver through fraudulent action on behalf of a company, then he or she may wind up in the courts or may take action like that. Nonetheless, this particular proposal would, it seems to me, at least avoid some of the most egregious and difficult problems we have had, particularly with companies that are just on the borderline and just outside the frontier of the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation or the provincial equivalent to provide deposit insurance to certain provincially-run institutions.
The resolution proposes that there should be co-operation with the provinces when dealing with those institutions that do not fall under federal jurisdiction directly. The federal Government should seek co-operation at the provincial level in order to make sure that shysters and fast-buck artists do not simply transfer their area of activities to the provincial level in order to avoid this measure being taken at the federal level.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to rise to say a few words in connection with this motion of the Elon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis), which is a request for the Government to consider the advisability of co-operating with the provinces in establishing a system whereby those individuals who deposit money in financial institutions not covered by deposit insurance be required to sign a waiver form indicating that they are fully aware that their deposits are not insured in the event that the institution goes bankrupt.
This is a very laudable motion. It deals, of course, with the question of consumer protection. That is something that I believe every one of us in the House can fully support. We support measures which will protect consumers, and particularly measures which will protect consumers of products of financial institutions.
All Hon. Members and all Canadians are aware that we have had problems in the recent past with financial institutions. I suppose the ones that come to my mind most readily are the failures of the Canadian Commercial Bank, the Northland Bank and the Principal Group in the West. All of these have been high-profile items in Parliament and across Canada. Certainly they have had an enormous impact on Canadians, regardless of whether or not they had deposits in those institutions.
Hon. Members will recall the debates that ranged in this House with respect to the Government's efforts to assist depositors in the Canadian Commercial Bank and in the Northland Bank. Those efforts were in fact the sorts of efforts that seem to be represented in the motion that is before us today. They were efforts to protect the consumers of the services of financial institutions.
I was disturbed, as I am sure you were, Mr. Speaker, by the attitude of members of the Opposition with respect to those efforts of the Government of Canada to protect consumers, and in particular, the attitude of members of the Opposition with respect to the failures of the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank. Members of the Opposition, Members who are putting forward this motion and are supporting this motion and the concept of consumer protection for depositors in financial institutions, in effect took great umbrage at the Government's efforts to protect consumers in those cases, and in fact characterized those consumer protection efforts on the part of the Government as being efforts to bail out the big investors in the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank. You and I, Mr. Speaker, know very well that that was not what was happening at all. In fact, the effort made on behalf of the Government, the successful effort, was an effort at consumer protection. It was an effort to protect the depositors in those banks.
Financial Institutions
While the depositors in those banks, to all intents and purposes, had huge deposits, those huge deposits represented the funds of a lot of little people. Those deposits included pension funds and deposits on behalf of credit unions. There were all sorts of large deposits which reflected the money of little people across Canada, the money of people who could not afford to lose their life savings if those banks went under. These people could not afford to lose their pension funds and the funds they had deposited in credit unions and institutions of that sort.
It was that effort on behalf of the Government to protect consumers in those cases that I personally believe was extremely laudable. I could not understand the attitude at that time of opposition Members in opposing those efforts and in trying to characterize them as some heinous crime rather than an effort to protect the average Canadian's savings through some sort of consumer protection for deposits in financial institutions.
In the case of the Principal Group failure, I also found it somewhat disconcerting to find that the argument of members of the Opposition had been reversed and flopped over. In that case, the Government clearly had a jurisdictional difficulty because the Principal Group was regulated provincially instead of federally, but now opposition Members were calling for exactly the opposite thing.
Instead of telling the Government that it should not help depositors, it was telling the Government that it should be rushing in to help with the Principal Group depositors, while in fact the Principal Group was a group of provincially-regulated institutions. It seemed inconsistent to me at that time. In fact, it seemed shocking to me that the Opposition would not want to protect consumers in the cases of the Northland Bank and the Canadian Commercial Bank but would want to have the Government protect consumers in the case of a financial institution which fell under provincial jurisdiction, not federal jurisdiction. That seemed inconsistent to me.
It seems even more inconsistent and inconceivable that here we now have a motion presented by the Hon. Member, laudable as it is, to protect consumers in this sort of a situation. While the principle is an outstanding one, and I certainly would be the last one to quarrel with it because I supported the Government in all of its efforts to protect consumers, I find it somewhat inconsistent and perhaps a little hypocritical to put forward this kind of a motion now.
Having said that, Mr. Speaker, you know and I know that Canadians are interested not in buck-passing, not in seeing one Government say it is somebody else's fault-"It is not our fault and we will not do anything"-Canadians are interested in seeing some action, making sure that whoever is in office as far as a Government is concerned, federally or provincially, that it acts in their best interests and does everything to protect them as best it can. That is what the Government has been

May 31, 1988
Financial Institutions
doing over the past four years or so since it took office in September, 1984.
The Government has introduced a number of measures to protect the consumer of the products of financial institutions, not only the ones to whom I have referred previously with respect to the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank, but it also issued a Green Paper in the spring, 1985, setting out some principles with respect to the regulation of financial institutions and the reform of the financial sector. Those principles, as you may recall, were as follows. First and foremost, it was to improve consumer protection; second, the strict control of self-dealing; third, to guard against abuses of conflict of interest; fourth, to promote competition, innovation and efficiency; fifth, to enhance the convenience and options available to consumers in the market-place; sixth, to broaden the sources of credit available to individuals and business; seventh, to ensure the soundness of financial institutions and the stability of financial systems; eighth, to promote international competitiveness and domestic economic growth; and ninth, to promote the harmonization of federal-provincial regulatory policies.
Embodied in those principles, first, is consumer protection, protecting the consumers of the services of financial institutions. As well, embodied in there is the principle of promoting harmony between federal and provincial regulatory policies. That, in effect, is the essence of the motion we are debating this evening. It is exactly that, and those are the principles on which the Government has been proceeding.
I see, Mr. Speaker, that you are signalling me that my time is running out. I wanted to point out a number of specific problems which this motion raises, notwithstanding that the principle is a laudatory one and one that I support, but I guess you are telling me that I do not have time to do so on this occasion. Perhaps Members of the House would give me unanimous consent to continue but if that is not the case, I will bow to your authority as members of the Opposition should have done a few moments ago.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to rise to speak on Motion No. 143 presented by the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis). I know I join Members on all sides of the House in applauding what I think is the general intent of the motion. The Hon. Member suggests in the motion that the Government of Canada, in co-operation with the provinces, establish a system where, in his words, individuals who deposit money in financial institutions not covered by deposit insurance be required to sign a waiver form indicating that they are fully aware that their deposits are not insured in the event the institution goes bankrupt.
In the context in which the Member introduced this motion, it is a motion for which he should be commended. Obviously, for those of us in western Canada who have seen some considerable difficulties develop over the past few years and the resulting difficulties that depositors have suffered, this motion is well intentioned. As well intentioned as it is, does this motion address clearly both the problem and the solution?
When a Member of Parliament talks with a person who has literally been bilked out of his or her entire life savings, it is obviously the type of situation which evinces from all of us not only compassion and sympathy but more than a little outrage. Obviously a Member of Parliament is very concerned that the Government serves to protect the depositors and serves to protect those involved in financial institutions. This motion as it is worded does not first identify the problem and clearly does not move toward the solution.
I would refer Hon. Members to a couple of recent Bills which the Government has passed, namely, Bill C-42 and C-56, both of which deal with the financial sector. One deals with the issue of deposits. We should look at the role of the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation. This is the cornerstone of the system for protecting depositors. No one other than a member institution of CDIC can represent itself as being insured by CDIC. This was the case even before Bill C-42. But the Government went further, and in that Bill we improved the supervisory powers of the CDIC and added three further elements to clarify and extend the scope of the supervisory powers of the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation. I want to touch briefly on those three points, Mr. Speaker.
First, there was some question regarding the extent of the prohibition on people making an unauthorized representation that their institution was covered by CDIC. The reforms now clearly indicate that the existing ban applies both to an institution and to all persons acting as agents for an institution. There is some clarity now in terms of prohibiting unauthorized representations from being made. Second, the regulations in Bill C-42 now state that this, assuming an uninsured deposit, must be indicated in writing by the institution on the deposit contract. This is a new feature of the legislation. Third, Bill C-42 extended to all members of the CDIC the requirement that institutions which solicit funds for investment on behalf of their investment company subsidiaries or other non-members of the CDIC must give notice to investors that such funds are not insured by CDIC.
Hon. Members will remember that during the debate on Bill C-42 we considered it in tandem with Bill C-56. Provisions of that legislation will help protect consumers who are not making conventional deposits but are, in effect, using depositlike instruments. This Bill lays the groundwork for the creation of protection plans in the insurance industry. The Government is working with representatives of the industry to develop annuity and policyholder protection plans that will extend the type of protection CDIC does with the chartered banks.
May 31, 1988

The Government has been actively pursuing other avenues as well. We are all aware that the future of the financial sector is going to be very different from its past. New associations of companies and functions have already started to appear, and I think we all expect, as time goes on, that there will be more in the way of services being offered to consumers and more flexibility as both technology and regulation progress. New instruments inevitably will be found, some of which will be very much like deposits which may not be protected under CDIC guidelines. There should exist the type of vehicle that other deposit instruments are protected by. For that reason, it is of paramount importance that we continue to work along with the provinces and along with the specific industries to ensure that protection exists.
I want to speak a little about the need for this type of motion and question whether it is required at this time. The Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap, when he introduced the motion, and I quote from a Globe and Mail story dated March 1, 1988, said:
As financial deregulation proceeds and competition for consumer deposits
increases, the temptation to mislead consumers greatly increases-
I guess that goes to the fundamental view one has of not only the financial community but of life itself.
Members of the NDP say that as one begins to open up competition, particularly in the financial sector, this will somehow turn human beings into essentially law-breaking, evil people who will be compelled to take advantage of others. That grossly oversimplifies the financial community and human nature. I do not think that one can assume, as a result of the moving of the four traditional pillars, that financial institutions are going to be out bilking the aged and those who are less able to protect themselves. If you accepted that faulty premise, as the NDP has, would you then suggest that the alternative is signing a piece of paper, a waiver?
We all know about the so-called fine print. All of us, in getting something as simple as a car loan all the way up to more complicated contracts with banks and financial institutions, routinely sign certain pieces of paper. In fact, this is an argument we have all been following with respect to bank service charges where people are given notice of bank charges and they sign documents which indicate they are willing to accept the service charges. Yet there is controversy.
My point is that if there is great evil in the world and people will be encouraged to bilk widows out of their life savings, would they not do it even if you compelled them to sign a piece of paper? Clearly they would. The answer to the problem has to be a careful analysis of what we find in Bill C-42 and Bill C-56 through increased supervisory powers of the CDIC and increased opportunity to find methods to provide CDIC-like insurance for other types of investment instruments.
I want it to be clear that the kind of spirit with which all concerned Members of Parliament deal with aggrieved
Financial Institutions
constituents, people who have indeed been misrepresented, leads us to be concerned to the extent that we move towards more progressive legislation. The Government has done that through Bill C-42 and Bill C-56. It also might lead Members, as the NDP has, to move to this signing of waivers.
In closing, I believe the way to go is to ensure that we have greater compliance, greater supervision, and while there might be a role at some point for this kind of approach, I do not believe it is suitable at this point. I think other Members want to speak on this issue and I will therefore yield to those who have some views on the usefulness of this type of motion and its place in the financial community.

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker, for allowing me to comment on this motion today. It raises a number of very appropriate questions about consumer protection and other aspects of the financial system, so I am happy to have this chance to speak. Nonetheless, I am not happy with certain assumptions it makes, and so I feel the House ought not to accept it.
This is now the third occasion on which we have had this motion before us, and Members opposite have ably expressed their opinions and not just about the subject of the motion. Their comments earlier in this debate are an attempt to criticize the federal Government for not exercising responsibility it does not have. The Hon. Member for Kamloops- Shuswap (Mr. Riis) wants the federal Government to assume an authority it does not have and intervene where it has no right to go. He wants us to take over the responsibilities of the Government which is responsible.
The previous Speaker referred to the Principal Group and comments in a newspaper article attributed to the mover of the motion. However, let us be very clear about this question of responsibility. Of the 127 different companies in the Principal Group, not one was federally regulated. Only one company, Principal Savings and Trust, was even a member of the CDIC. That Corporation moved quickly to discharge its responsibilities. In just over three weeks it arranged to pay out the insured deposits of 47,000 depositors through an agency agreement with Metropolitan Trust. Total pay-outs on that account have reached $116 million.
I have no trouble with the motion's call for co-operation between the provinces and the federal Government on consumer protection. Our reforms have set an example. We are proud of the work we are doing in this sector because we know that a new regime is necessary to ensure protection of the interests of depositors, borrowers and shareholders. Yet we cannot take responsibility for what is outside our jurisdiction. The federal Government has no desire to intrude on provincial jurisdiction. However, as a Government we hope the provincial authorities will study our regime carefully and work with us to ensure thorough and capable measures for all consumers throughout Canada.

May 31, 1988
Non-smokers' Health Act
I now want to turn to the reforms we have carried out already in the financial sector, reforms which have already strengthened the consumer protection regime. Bill C-42 and Bill C-56 made major changes to the regulatory framework in response to the demands of the institutions and the needs of consumers. We instituted the office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions and made important changes to the CDIC. We will be proceeding as quickly as possible with changes to the Trust and Loans Companies Act, the Insurance Companies Act, and other Acts to ensure that consumers are protected and the sector encouraged.
Even prior to these reforms, a non-member of CDIC was prohibited from representing itself as being insured by the CDIC. There has been a requirement for some time that uninsured instruments should be stamped as such. Bill C-42 added three important further elements to these measures.
First, it cleared up a question about the existing ban on unauthorized representations of insured status of member institutions or deposits received by them. This ban now clearly applies both to the institution and all persons acting as its agents.
Second, the Bill put into the Act a provision previously in the regulations. It is now a statutory requirement that when an institution takes a deposit which is not insured, this must be indicated in writing on the deposit contract.
Third, it instituted a new requirement that institutions, which solicit funds for investment on behalf of their investment company subsidiaries or other non-members of the CDIC must give notice to investors that these companies are non-members and that such funds are not insured by the CDIC. The draft trust and loans legislation takes account of this by enabling the Governor in Council to make regulations imposing terms and conditions on the activities that companies undertake in the areas open to them. Similar provisions will be incorporated in the legislation governing banks and insurance companies.
I see that my time is running out. I was going to comment further on Bill C-56 but I will conclude with this. I believe that what is now in place, and those provisions now being implemented, will provide an appropriate degree of protection for consumers, that is depositors, borrowers and investors. I believe our approach to the question's federal-provincial dimension is also sound; we are not trying to impose our solution but are trying to work out a mutually agreeable solution. I am confident that our Government's approach is a good one.
